Babylonian Captivity
bab-uh-LOH-nee-uhn kap-TIV-i-tee
noun (historical, redemptive-historical)
From Babylon, the Chaldean empire on the Euphrates, and Latin captivitas, the state of being held as a prisoner of war; the term names the deportation of Judah to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar.

See also: Babylonian Captivity

📖 Biblical Definition

The Babylonian Captivity was the seventy-year exile of the kingdom of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar burnt the house of the LORD and carried the people away from their land (2 Kings 25). It was no accident of empire but the righteous judgment of God upon a covenant people who had broken His covenant, despised His prophets, and gone whoring after idols. Jeremiah had foretold both the length and the meaning of it: "And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jer 25:11). Daniel, reading the prophet, understood the term by the books (Dan 9:2) and turned to confession and supplication. Yet judgment was not the last word. God preserved a remnant in the furnace, kept His promise to David, and brought His people home again, that the Seed might come. The captivity therefore stands as a sober type of the deeper bondage of sin and of the redemption wrought by Christ, who leads captivity captive. This dictionary confesses that God chastens His own in faithfulness, never in caprice, and that even His severest providences serve His covenant of grace.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The seventy-year deportation of Judah to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, sent as the righteous judgment of God for covenant-breaking and idolatry. A remnant was preserved and restored, and the captivity stands as a type of bondage to sin and redemption in Christ.

expand to see more

BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY, noun. The carrying away of the kingdom of Judah into Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and their bondage there for seventy years.

It was the judicial sentence of God upon a nation that had filled the cup of its iniquity with idolatry and the shedding of innocent blood.

"And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jer 25:11).

The captivity required of Judah the just wages of covenant-breaking, yet it preserved a remnant for the promise.

Its sanction is the faithfulness of God, who both chastens and restores His covenant people in mercy.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Kings 25:8-9 — "And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: And he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire."

Jer 25:11 — "And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years."

Dan 9:2 — "In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem."

2 Chron 36:20 — "And them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon; where they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The chief corruption is to read the exile as mere political misfortune or imperial accident, emptying it of its character as the righteous judgment of God.

expand to see more

Critical reconstruction often treats the captivity as a sociological event to be explained by geopolitics alone, and treats the prophets as men reinterpreting disaster after the fact rather than foretelling it by the Spirit. Scripture forbids this. Jeremiah named both the cause and the seventy-year measure before it came to pass, and Daniel read those very words as inspired and dated. To strip the exile of its moral and prophetic meaning is to deny that God governs the nations and chastens His people in covenant faithfulness.

The believer recovers the true principle: God is not mocked, and a people that despises His word and bows to idols will reap what it has sown. Yet the same God who sends the furnace preserves a remnant within it and brings them home in His appointed time. The captivity thus teaches both the severity and the goodness of God, and points beyond itself to the redemption from sin's bondage accomplished in Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The term joins the name of Babylon to the Latin idea of captivity, naming Judah's seventy-year bondage as a covenant sentence.

expand to see more

Babylon — Heb. Babel, the Chaldean city and empire upon the Euphrates, long a biblical figure of pride and confusion.

Captivity — from Latin captivitas, the condition of one taken and held by a conqueror.

The seventy years are fixed by Jeremiah and confirmed by Daniel, a measured, not arbitrary, chastisement.

The deportation came in stages, culminating in the burning of the temple in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year.

Scripture reads the whole as judgment in righteousness and restoration in mercy, both governed by God.

Usage

"The Babylonian Captivity was the harvest of generations of idolatry, reaped at last under Nebuchadnezzar."

"Daniel counted the years of the Babylonian Captivity from the books of Jeremiah and fell to prayer."

"Even in the Babylonian Captivity God kept a remnant, that the promise to David should not fail."
